html:
A law passed by New Zealand's first Labour government in 1938 that set up one of the world's first full welfare states, with pensions, benefits and free health care for all.

Labour, led by Michael Joseph Savage, had won power in 1935 after the hardship of the Great Depression. Savage called the scheme "applied Christianity". The act brought in a universal old age payment, benefits for the sick, widows, orphans, the unemployed and families, and free hospital care and medicines, paid for by a special social security tax on income. The doctors resisted parts of the plan, and free visits to family doctors came in more slowly.

The act was praised abroad as the most complete social security system of its time. It helped make New Zealand known as a "social laboratory", after earlier reforms such as votes for women in 1893. Britain's welfare state after the Second World War took up similar ideas. The Labour Party passed it with the support of its Māori allies of the Rātana movement. See New Zealand.
sum: A law passed by New Zealand's first Labour government in 1938 that set up one of the world's first full welfare states, with pensions, benefits and free health care for all.
